channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.6% in October from 3.5% in September, below the 3.7% expected, with motor fuel prices 33.2% higher than a year earlier, and the Bank of England expects inflation to rise further by the middle of next year.
item.description:
UK consumer price inflation rose from 3.5% in September to 3.6% in October, the Office for National Statistics reports; the ONS cited a 33.2% annual rise in fuel prices for motorists, with petrol averaging 174.7p a litre in October, up 5.2p from September, and diesel 199.5p, up 7p, The Guardian reports. The rate was below the 3.7% market consensus, and services inflation was 3.7%, below the 3.8% consensus and the 3.9% the Bank of England projected in its November Monetary Policy Report, MarketScreener reports. Investors trimmed bets on a Bank of England rate rise next month as some underlying components held steady. A Bank of England spokesperson said the conflict in the Middle East has raised energy prices and inflation in recent months and that inflation is expected to rise further because of cost pressures already in the pipeline. Governor Andrew Bailey said interest rates are not on a pre-set path, and that the longer the conflict keeps energy prices high, the more likely persistent inflation effects become and the higher rates will need to be. The rows do not give core inflation, food prices or producer prices.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The ONS cited fuel prices as a factor in the rise; services inflation came in below forecasts, and the Bank of England's statement is an expectation. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, energy costs passing into consumer prices with a lag keep inflation above target into 2027 and leave the timing of rate rises dependent on the war, which weighs on household spending and housing activity. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, UK construction, car and consumer demand depend on financing costs and real incomes, and transport and energy costs feed into raw material and distribution costs. Points that may be worth considering include the Bank of England's December decision, UK producer prices and fuel prices.

The Guardian | MarketScreener | MarketScreener | MarketScreener

item.title: Minutes of the Fed's 27–28 October meeting show almost all policymakers saw further rate rises as needed if the economy evolves as they expect, and Governor Waller favours a half-point rise in December unless a January rise is clearly signalled.
item.description:
According to the minutes of the Federal Reserve's meeting on 27–28 October, almost all policymakers agreed that further rate rises would be needed if the economy evolved as they expected, and a few said inflation could prove more persistent and require a more restrictive stance than currently expected, The Economic Times reports. The Fed held its policy rate in the 3.75%–4.00% range; Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favour of a quarter-point rise. A couple of participants noted that an increase of more than 25 basis points could be considered at the next meeting in case of unfavourable inflation data, Il Sole 24 Ore reports. On 18 November Governor Christopher Waller said he favours a half-point rise in December unless policymakers clearly signal that a quarter-point rise would be followed by another in January, AA reports; rate futures fully priced a quarter-point rise in December, with traders also expecting another in January. Inflation data for the past three months suggest an annualised rate of around 3.5%, The Economic Times reports. The FOMC meets on 8 and 9 December, and Bank Indonesia raised its rate by 25 basis points to 6% on 18 November in anticipation of a Fed rise, The Jakarta Post reports.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The minutes and Waller's remarks are statements, not decisions; the market already prices a quarter-point rise. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a larger or faster US tightening raises borrowing costs for housing, cars and capital equipment and tends to strengthen the dollar, which makes dollar-priced raw materials more expensive outside the US, and Bank Indonesia has already raised its rate ahead of an expected Fed rise. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, US construction and automotive demand depend on financing costs, so the size of the December step matters for 2027 volumes. Points that may be worth considering include the 9 December decision, the next US inflation data and rate moves in emerging markets.

The Economic Times | Il Sole 24 Ore | AA | The Economic Times | Jakarta Post

item.title: The EU institutions agreed to delay by two years, to 1 January 2029, rules requiring oil, gas and coal importers to report methane emissions, because of disruption from the US-Israeli war with Iran.
item.description:
The EU and the European Parliament have agreed to delay by two years rules requiring oil, gas and coal importers to report methane emissions, because of the disruptions from the US-Israeli war with Iran, MarketScreener reports. The two-year delay is longer than the European Commission's proposal in October for a one-year delay to the methane emissions rules for oil and gas imports, and followed pressure from governments including France and from the United States. The rules were due to take effect on 1 January 2027; the co-legislators have agreed to a start date of 1 January 2029. The row does not say whether the content of the rules changes, which supplier countries would have been most affected, or when the delay is formally adopted.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

This is a change to the timing of a reporting rule, not a change in energy prices or volumes. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, postponing reporting duties for importers removes a compliance hurdle that could have narrowed the list of usable oil and gas suppliers from 2027, at a time when the war has already disrupted supply. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, European energy and petrochemical feedstock costs depend on the range of import sources, so a wider supplier base in 2027 and 2028 supports supply security, while the delay also postpones the point at which importers must report methane emissions. Points that may be worth considering include the formal adoption of the delay, any changes to the 2029 requirements and supplier responses.

MarketScreener

item.title: US Central Command said ships that receive cargo at sea from vessels loaded in Iran will be treated as attempting to evade the US naval blockade of Iranian ports and could face enforcement action.
item.description:
According to an advisory issued by US Central Command (CENTCOM) on Wednesday, ships that receive cargo at sea from vessels loaded in Iran will be treated by the US military as attempting to evade its blockade of Iranian ports, and it could take action against them, Arab News reports. Ships that fail to comply immediately with lawful orders from blockade or boarding forces could face enforcement action, including the use of force consistent with applicable law. The blockade on Iran-related oil exports was first imposed on 13 April, lifted in June after a draft understanding with Tehran, and reimposed on 14 July after the agreement collapsed. The US military again has two aircraft carriers supporting Iran war operations, the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS Theodore Roosevelt, along with more than a dozen destroyers, cruisers and a littoral combat ship, after the USS George Washington moved to the Asia-Pacific, AP reports. Oil prices fell as expectations of an oversupplied market and bearish US inventory data outweighed continued tanker attacks in the Middle East; in early European trading Brent fell 1.9% to USD 91.38 a barrel, MarketScreener reports. The rows do not say how many ships or barrels are moved by transfers at sea.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The advisory widens the scope of enforcement; the rows give no measured effect on oil flows, and the oil price fell on the day. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, transfers at sea are a route by which blockaded cargoes can reach buyers, so treating them as evasion raises the risk for shipowners and buyers of such cargoes and may reduce the volume that leaves Iran this way. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, oil-derived feedstocks and freight costs carry the war's risk premium, and on the day the market weighed expected oversupply and US inventory data more heavily than continued tanker attacks. Points that may be worth considering include enforcement incidents, the response of buyers in Asia and the oil price.

Arab News | AP | MarketScreener

item.title: Germany's governing coalition agreed to cut the electricity tax from 2.05 cents to 0.1 cent per kilowatt-hour for households and businesses that have not yet had a reduction, for 2027 for the time being.
item.description:
On 18 November, Germany's coalition of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Union bloc and the Social Democrats agreed to reduce electricity taxes for all consumers and businesses, AP reports. When they formed the coalition 18 months ago, the parties agreed in principle to cut electricity taxes to the minimum level allowed under EU rules, but so far have reduced the levies only for industry and agriculture. The coalition leaders agreed to cut the tax from 2.05 cents per kilowatt-hour to 0.1 cent for households and businesses that have yet to receive a reduction. The cut applies only to 2027 for the time being and will be funded with surplus money earmarked for renewable energy; funding for 2028 and beyond has yet to be agreed. Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung writes that after the state elections in September the cut was portrayed as a symbol of the CDU's assertiveness, and that because the Iran war is driving up electricity prices via the oil and gas market, funds that would otherwise subsidise solar and wind power can be used to reduce electricity prices. The rows do not give the cost of the measure or the saving for an average household or business.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The cut reaches households and businesses that have not yet had a reduction; industry and agriculture have already had their levies reduced. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a lower electricity tax for households and the remaining businesses in 2027 eases household energy bills and small-business costs at a time of high energy prices, and the open funding question for 2028 leaves relief beyond 2027 uncertain. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, consumers, craftsmen and trade customers in the home market are the users of construction and do-it-yourself products, so their energy costs and spending power bear on renovation demand. Points that may be worth considering include the funding decision for 2028, the size of the saving per household and any further energy relief for industry.

AP | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: EU governments authorised the signature and provisional application of the EU–Indonesia trade deal, under which both sides are to remove import duties on more than 90% of products and Indonesia's 50% duty on EU cars is to be eliminated within five years.
item.description:
European Union governments authorised on Wednesday the signature and provisional application of a previously agreed trade deal between the EU and Indonesia, The Jakarta Post reports. The deal, initially concluded in September 2025, will see both sides remove import duties on more than 90% of products, most of them as soon as the deal enters into force. Indonesia's 50% duty on EU cars will be eliminated within five years. These agreements will remove tariffs on almost all goods traded between the EU and Indonesia and save businesses an estimated EUR 600 million a year in customs duties, said Irish foreign affairs and trade minister Helen McEntee. The row does not give a date for the signature or for provisional application, the product schedules, the rules of origin or the trade volumes concerned.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The decision authorises signature and provisional application; the row gives no date for either. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a deal that removes duties on more than 90% of products gives EU exporters of cars, machinery and chemicals easier access to a large Southeast Asian market, and lowers the cost of Indonesian goods imported into the EU. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the phase-out of the 50% car duty and lower duties on industrial goods could shift where automotive and electronics customers build and source in the region, and lower duties on chemical inputs could change supply options. Points that may be worth considering include the signature date, the duty schedules for chemicals and adhesive raw materials, and the rules of origin.

Jakarta Post

item.title: ASE Technology plans to invest USD 3.05 billion in two new plants in Kaohsiung, and its unit SPIL signed a multi-year deal with Nvidia to triple its high-throughput monolithic advanced packaging capacity in Taiwan by mid-2029.
item.description:
On 17 November, semiconductor packaging and testing provider ASE Technology announced that it would invest USD 3.05 billion in two new manufacturing facilities in Kaohsiung, Taiwan, to meet rising demand for AI and high-performance computing chips, Supply Chain Digital reports; it also confirmed that Nvidia plans to invest several billion US dollars to expand chip-on-wafer-on-substrate (CoWoS) capacity at ASE's unit Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL). On 18 November SPIL said it had signed a multi-billion-dollar, multi-year agreement with Nvidia to expand its high-throughput monolithic advanced packaging capacity in Taiwan, including a new production line covering wafer bumping, packaging and testing; capacity will be expanded to three times its current size by mid-2029, Cnyes reports. On 19 November ASE subsidiary Taiwan Folei Electronics broke ground on a new J Block plant in Kaohsiung, with an additional investment of TWD 248.9 billion and phased completion between 2028 and 2029, Commercial Times reports. Nvidia reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of USD 115.8 billion, up 103% year on year, and expects about USD 130 billion in the fourth quarter, AA reports. The rows do not give capacity in units or the value of the Nvidia agreement.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

These are investment plans and a contracted capacity target, not current output; the rows do not say whether the two investment figures overlap, so they are not added here. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a tripling of SPIL's advanced packaging capacity by mid-2029 under an agreement with Nvidia shows how far demand for AI chips is expected to run, and capacity in this step of chipmaking has been one of the limits on AI server supply. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, advanced chip packaging uses underfills, die-attach materials, encapsulants and thermal interface materials, so added packaging lines in Taiwan raise demand for qualified electronics materials there over the next three years. Points that may be worth considering include the ramp-up schedule, capacity plans at other packaging groups and the qualification of materials for new lines.

Supply Chain Digital | Cnyes | Commercial Times | AA

item.title: Building permits for apartments in Germany fell by nearly 15% to 20,800 in September, and for new-build apartments by 19.9% to 16,800, ending an upward trend, Federal Statistical Office data show.
item.description:
The number of building permits in Germany fell by nearly 15% to 20,800 apartments in September 2026, and approvals for new-build apartments fell by 19.9% to 16,800, according to the Federal Statistical Office in Wiesbaden, Handelsblatt and Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung report. Between January and August, approvals for apartments had increased by a good 12%. In the first three quarters, permits were issued for 190,200 apartments in new and existing buildings, up 8.4% year on year; in new buildings the number rose 8.0%, with particularly large increases in two-family houses (17.7%) and multi-family houses (9.3%), Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reports. Both outlets report that, with the Iran war, higher energy prices and more expensive materials are burdening developers, and interest rates for ten-year real estate loans have risen above 4%. Felix Pakleppa, General Manager of the Central Association of the German Construction Industry (ZDB), said construction interest rates are currently 4.4%, nearly four times as high as ten years ago, Handelsblatt reports. The rows do not state the comparison base for the September fall, a regional split or permits for non-residential buildings.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Permits are approvals, not construction starts or completions, and the nine-month total is still above the same period of last year. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a sharp fall in one month after a rise of a good 12% in January–August can be a turning point or a single weak month, and permits usually lead building activity by several months, so the effect would show in 2027 rather than now. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, residential building uses tile adhesives, sealants, flooring and insulation materials, so the permit trend bears on construction demand in the home market next year, while renovation of existing buildings follows its own drivers. Points that may be worth considering include the October permit data, mortgage rates and whether new-build and existing-building approvals move apart.

Handelsblatt | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: US single-family housing starts rose 4.0% in October to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 864,000, while homebuilding was 3.2% lower than a year earlier, and single-family permits fell 8.7%, to their lowest since January 2023, Census Bureau data show.
item.description:
Single-family housing starts in the US increased 4.0% to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 864,000 units in October, according to the Commerce Department's Census Bureau, Yahoo reports. On a year-on-year basis, homebuilding declined 3.2%. Building permits for single-family housing projects declined 8.7% to a rate of 772,000 units, the lowest level since January 2023. The row does not give multi-family starts, total starts, completions or a regional split, nor a reason for the moves.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Starts measure building begun in the month, and here starts and permits move in opposite directions. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a monthly rise in starts alongside permits at their lowest since January 2023 suggests builders are working through approved projects while approving fewer new ones, which tends to weigh on activity in the coming months. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, single-family homes use sealants, flooring, roofing, window and insulation materials, so a lower permit level points to softer US residential demand into 2027, with mortgage rates and the Fed's December decision as the main swing factors. Points that may be worth considering include November permits and starts, mortgage rates and builders' order intake.

Yahoo

item.title: Chemical plant closures in Europe have surged sixfold since 2022, and cumulative closed capacity has reached 37 Mt, about 9% of European production capacity, a Roland Berger report commissioned by Cefic shows.
item.description:
The European Chemical Industry Council (Cefic) has published a 2026 report, commissioned from Roland Berger, which finds that chemical plant closures in Europe surged sixfold since 2022 and reached a cumulative 37 Mt of capacity, around 9% of European production capacity. Cefic says the chemical sector directly employs more than 1.2 million people in the EU27 and accounts for around 7% of total manufacturing value added, and that, as part of the energy-intensive industries, it is strongly exposed to energy prices. It attributes the adjustment since 2022 to the sharp increase in energy costs combined with intensifying global competition. The period is characterised by a simultaneous decline in both emissions and production levels across several EU countries, alongside increasing reports of capacity reductions and site closures. The rows do not give a split by country, product chain or year, name the plants that closed, or say how much new capacity opened in the same period.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The 37 Mt is cumulative closed capacity, not lost output or sales, and the rows do not say how much of it was running before closure. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, closures of this scale reduce the number of European producers of base and intermediate chemicals and raise the share of supply that must come from outside Europe. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, many resins, polymers and solvents come from European chemical value chains, so closures can change sourcing options, supplier concentration and lead times, and falling emissions, where they reflect lower activity rather than efficiency, say little about the cost position of the plants that remain. Points that may be worth considering include which product chains the closures affect, how much of the affected raw material supply can be sourced outside Europe, and further closure announcements.

Cefic | Cefic
